name: Event streams
summary: An append-only log of events that many readers replay at their own pace.
howItWorks: Producers append records to the end of a log that’s kept for a retention period: hours, days or forever. Reading removes nothing. Each consumer group tracks its own position, called an offset, so a real-time alerting job, a dashboard and a nightly batch can all read the same data independently. Logs are split into partitions for scale, and order is guaranteed within a partition.
analogy: A DVR recording of live TV. You can watch live, pause, or rewind to this morning, and your roommate can be at a different point in the same recording.
useWhen: High-volume telemetry, clickstreams and IoT readings
Several independent consumers of the same events
Reprocessing history after a bug fix or to build a new view
avoidWhen: Simple job distribution where each task runs once; a queue is simpler
Low volume, where running a stream platform is more work than it saves
example: Thousands of well sensors publish pressure readings to a `readings` topic. Alerting reads each one within a second, the dashboard updates every few seconds, and the ML team replays the whole week on Sunday to retrain a model.

diagram.caption: Records stay in the log after they’re read. Three consumer groups move through the same records at different speeds; the ML job falls behind, then catches up in batches.

story: Before event streams, companies moved data between systems with one-off pipelines. At LinkedIn around 2010, Jay Kreps recalled, “we built jerry-rigged piping between systems and applications on an as needed basis,” and the complexity meant “the data was always unreliable.” Off-the-shelf brokers such as ActiveMQ were hard to scale, and dumps into Hadoop arrived in batches rather than in real time.

In 2010 LinkedIn decided to build one system for streams of data: Apache Kafka, open-sourced in 2011. The team called it “the global commit log thingy”: an ordered, append-only record that every system could write to and read from at its own pace. Amazon Kinesis offered the same model as a managed cloud service in 2013, and Apache Pulsar, which keeps storage separate from its brokers, became a top-level Apache project in 2018. Retention grew from hours to months, so a stream became a durable record that new systems could replay from the start.
Streams and queues have since converged from both sides: RabbitMQ added streams in 2021, and Kafka made queue-style share groups production-ready in 2026.

choices.why: Records stay for a retention period whoever has read them, so a dashboard, an alerting job and a nightly batch can all consume the same data, and a bug fix can be followed by a replay.

choices.choice: Each consumer keeps its own position
choices.why: The log doesn’t track delivery per message, so adding readers is cheap, and a reader can rewind just by moving its offset.

choices.choice: Partitions for scale, order within each
choices.why: Splitting a log across machines lets it grow; promising order only within a partition (one device, one user) avoids a global bottleneck.
Appending to the end of a file is the fastest thing a disk does, which lets a log absorb very high write rates on ordinary hardware.

timeline.text: LinkedIn starts building Kafka to replace ad hoc pipelines
Amazon Kinesis brings managed streams to the cloud
Apache Pulsar becomes a top-level Apache project
Kinesis retention can be extended to 365 days
Kafka 4.2 makes queue-style share groups production-ready
